opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is moving from a single line of defense to genuine defense in depth. Right now a lot of deployed systems rely mostly on safety training of the model itself, refusal behavior learned through fine-tuning. Our research and others' has shown that this is pretty brittle. Given enough attempts or a clever enough prompt, you can almost always find a way through. So if that's your only barrier, you're in trouble.

What you want instead is several layers that fail in different ways. You have the model's own training. You have input classifiers that look at what's coming in. You have output classifiers that check what's actually being generated, which matters because an attacker can disguise the request but it's much harder to disguise a harmful answer. And then you have monitoring at the account and conversation level, so you're not just judging each message in isolation but noticing when someone is clearly probing the system over hundreds of queries.

The catch is that defense in depth only works if the layers are actually independent. If an attacker can find one trick that fools the model and the classifiers at the same time, maybe because they're built on similar models or trained on similar data, you haven't gained as much as you think. So I'd encourage developers to red-team the whole stack together, not each component separately, and to assume the attacker can learn about the system over time.

The second big opportunity is just taking adversarial robustness seriously as a research problem rather than patching individual jailbreaks as they show up on social media. Patching is whack-a-mole. Adversarial training helps, but it tends to generalize poorly to new kinds of attacks. We need more investment in methods that hold up against adaptive attackers, and in honest evaluations that report how much effort it actually takes to break a system.

Third, I'd point to access controls and the deployment surface. A lot of the risk comes from capabilities like fine-tuning APIs, very long contexts, or tool use, which open new attack vectors. Developers can be more thoughtful about who gets access to the most sensitive capabilities, with things like know-your-customer checks for higher-risk uses.

And finally, transparency. Labs could share more about what attacks they're seeing and what's working defensively. Attackers share techniques freely, so defenders working in silos are at a disadvantage. If the field could coordinate better, maybe through third-party testing or shared benchmarks for robustness, I think we'd make much faster progress.

r001.rationale: The response recommends defense in depth by combining model training, input and output classifiers, and account- and conversation-level monitoring.

r002.rationale: It discusses account-level monitoring and KYC checks for higher-risk uses, but does not say to limit attackers’ ability to create arbitrarily many accounts.

r003.rationale: It mentions KYC, but does not identify minimum-spend requirements as a privacy-preserving alternative to identity verification.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by saying that I think the single biggest lever is defense in depth. For a long time the implicit assumption in the field was that you'd train the model itself to be robust, and that would be the whole story. And what we've learned, both from our own red-teaming at FAR.AI and from the broader academic literature, is that no single model, however well trained, is going to be robust to a motivated adversary who has unlimited query access. The attack surface is just too large. So the question becomes: what can you layer around the model?

The first layer that I think is underexploited is input and output classifiers. These are cheap, they're fast, and critically they can be trained on a different distribution than the base model, so an attack that works on one often doesn't transfer to the other. Anthropic's constitutional classifiers work is a good example of this actually starting to be deployed at scale. They're not perfect, but they raise the cost of attack substantially, and cost is really what we care about here. We're not going to get to zero jailbreaks, but if we can move from "a bored teenager finds one in an afternoon" to "it takes a well-resourced team weeks," that's a meaningful change in the risk profile.

The second opportunity is around monitoring and response at the account level rather than the query level. Right now a lot of defenses treat each request independently. But real attackers iterate. They probe, they get a refusal, they tweak, they try again. That pattern is actually quite detectable if you're looking for it. So rate limiting on suspicious behavior, escalating friction for accounts that keep hitting refusals, and in some cases just banning accounts, is a very powerful tool that doesn't require any advance in machine learning. It's a product and operations decision.

Third, I think there's a lot of room in red-teaming methodology itself. Most labs do red-teaming, but it's often relatively ad hoc and relies heavily on human creativity. Automated attack generation has gotten quite good, and I'd like to see labs run those systematically before deployment, ideally with external parties who don't share the developers' blind spots. The adversary isn't going to politely restrict themselves to the threat models you thought of.

And then finally, there's the structural point: be honest about what the model is safe for. If you have a capability that would be genuinely dangerous if jailbroken, say serious uplift on bioweapons, you shouldn't be relying on the model's own refusals to protect against that. You should be thinking about whether that capability needs to be in a broadly deployed product at all, or whether it should be gated behind know-your-customer requirements and much tighter access controls. The defense that works best against jailbreaks is often not deploying the thing you can't defend.

r001.rationale: The response advocates defense in depth, layering classifiers, account-level monitoring, red-teaming, and access controls to raise the cost of jailbreak attacks.

r002.rationale: It proposes rate limits, friction, and bans for suspicious accounts, but does not discuss restricting attackers from creating arbitrarily many accounts.

r003.rationale: It does not mention minimum-spend requirements or present them as an alternative to identity verification.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most promising opportunities is to make the training process much more adversarial. Rather than just training on a collection of known jailbreaks, you want to actively search for attacks that work against the model you have today, train against those, and then repeat. The important question is whether that produces defenses that generalize to new attacks, rather than just teaching the model to recognize particular phrases.

And I’d put a lot of emphasis on the quality of the attacker you’re evaluating against. If your red team fails to find a jailbreak, that could mean you have a robust model, or it could mean your red team wasn’t searching effectively. Giving attackers more time, different strategies, and access to information about the defense can help distinguish those possibilities.

The other opportunity is at the system level. We shouldn’t expect the model to be the sole security boundary. If it can access sensitive data or take consequential actions, there should be permissions and checks around those capabilities. Then a jailbreak doesn’t automatically turn into a serious compromise. I’d want developers investing in both: making the models harder to manipulate, and limiting what happens when manipulation succeeds.

r001.rationale: The response recommends investing in both model-level defenses and system-level permissions and checks, combining complementary approaches to improve jailbreak resistance.

r002.rationale: It does not mention limiting attackers’ ability to create accounts.

r003.rationale: It does not mention minimum-spend requirements or identity verification as account-level defenses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most promising opportunities is to make the attacker’s job harder at the system level, rather than relying entirely on the model to refuse the right requests. If an AI agent can access sensitive information or take actions, you want permissions and isolation that limit what it can do even when someone successfully manipulates it. A jailbreak shouldn’t automatically become a compromise of everything the agent can access.

There’s also a lot of room to improve adversarial training and evaluation. You want to actively search for attacks, train against them, and then test whether the defenses generalize to attacks you haven’t seen before. Fixing a particular prompt is useful, but the more important question is whether you’ve addressed the underlying failure mode.

And I’d like to see developers make greater use of independent testing. Outside researchers bring different approaches and assumptions, which helps uncover blind spots. The goal should be a process where finding a new attack leads to a broader improvement in robustness, with additional safeguards for the failures that remain.

r001.rationale: The response recommends several complementary defenses—system-level permissions and isolation, adversarial training and evaluation, and independent testing—as ways to improve jailbreak resistance.

r002.rationale: It does not mention limiting how many accounts an attacker can create.

r003.rationale: It does not mention minimum-spend requirements or identity verification.
